newsitem.title: USA: Travelers will pay for quality.
newsitem.headline: Travelers will pay for quality.

text.p: Even with rising airfares and increased hotel costs, business travelers are willing to foot the bill, provided the value is there.
That's the view of Lisa Henriques, publisher of Conde Naste Traveller, the respected travel magazine that marks its 10th anniversary with its May 1997 issue.
"I think the travel industry has grown exponentially and absolutely has responded to consumer demand," she said in a telephone interview from Beijing, where she was -- what else -- travelling.

"American travelers and specifically business travelers were chastened by the stock market crash of 1987 and overnight consumers in general became more demanding. They wanted more value for their money, and certainly the travel industry responded," she said.

"What we've found now is that our readers are willing to pay high prices ... if they feel they're getting the value," Henriques said, adding that value can be a business centre, with favourable rates for family, weekend stay-overs and the like.

The travel industry, she aded, "is booming. The world is generally at peace, the dollar is strong, technology is strong ... hotels in any major city in the United States are operating at 90 percent capacity."

The magazine's anniversary issue offers a number of tips for travelers. Here are some it puts forth for those frequently on the road, collected, it says, from a select group of heavy business travelers:

-- If your flight is cancelled or delayed, don't wait in line at the gate. Head for a pay phone and book another flight on your airline's toll-free number (assuming you haven't checked luggage of course).
-- Avoid flying on Mondays, Fridays and Sundays and in general late in the day (admittedly a hard goal given the way business travel often falls).
-- If you've reached premium frequent flier status on one airline, approach a rival carrier and ask for the same thing. Some will offer to match the status, free, in hopes of luring a convert.
-- Carry an extension cord. Despite increasing sensitivity in the lodging industry to in-room work, many power plugs are still a far reach for laptop computers.
-- Resereve a rental car in which smoking is not allowed. In general, it said, these tend to be the newest cars in the fleet.
-- Hit the car rental counter at the airport before picking up your luggage, just in case they're overbooked.

Henriques said her magazine, whose circulation is at 750,000, has been successful because it has stressed "truth in travel," reported by writers who do their work unannounced and not on junkets sponsored by the industry.
